1:
Whether the inquiry was honest is the tile's question. Calvin says they acted more culpably in coming than if they had gone straight to Egypt, since they either dissembled or were so stupefied by hypocrisy as to lose their understanding; he generalises it, that a man asking counsel ought to bring no prejudice, whereas nothing is more common than to deliberate about a thing already settled, since those who consult mostly wish not to learn what is right but that others should fall in with their inclinations. Gill agrees they had set their faces toward Egypt and wanted only the Lord's sanction. Henry reads it the same way, the prophet being sought out at length only to serve a turn, their coming near betraying how far off they had kept till then. Clarke allows them more, holding they really did not know which way was safest and wished God's mind on the point though they inclined to Egypt. Ellicott allows them most, since they turn to him acknowledging a true prophet and trusting his patriotism, in a position truly difficult and dangerous.

How they addressed him matters as much. Henry finds the words wonderfully well chosen, since men who had the prophet under their command approach as petitioners, which he suspects was meant to persuade him to say what they wanted; and hears in the phrase about the Lord thy God a confession that they were unworthy to call God their own. Calvin explains it differently, that they were neither disowning God nor exempting themselves from his authority but extolling the prophet as God's true and lawful messenger, and observes that the admission recoiled on their own head, for if he was God's prophet they ought to have obeyed at once. He takes the plea about being left few of many for an appeal to pity.

The setting is filled in. Keil and Delitzsch place the halt near Bethlehem; Gill names the lodging on the road to Egypt and calls their fear of the Chaldeans a pretence. Keil and Delitzsch add a sharp note on the ten days before the answer came: two scholars make the delay the prophet's own, waiting on a conviction matured by meditation, which they reject as resting on a denial of inspiration. Ellicott works one of the names, suspecting that the man here is the brother of another named in the next chapter, and notes that the Greek gives that other name in this verse and may well be right.

What they undertook is defined three ways. Gill guards the phrase, since nothing morally evil can come from God, and restricts it to what is agreeable or disagreeable, profitable or not, in their own esteem. Wesley puts the same in two words, grateful or ungrateful to us. Calvin turns it into the test of fidelity itself: the one way to prove ourselves is to hold the word binding whether it pleases us or not, and never to murmur as the ungodly do when a yoke is laid on them.

The oath they added drew nothing but suspicion. Gill calls it a solemn appeal to a God faithful to his threatenings as to his promises, and marks the atheism of a professing people swearing what they never meant to perform while the judgments on their nation stood before their eyes. Clarke takes the appeal at its word, since the Lord is such a witness and will register the covenant and bless or curse accordingly. Calvin notices what the others pass over, that the prophet had not asked for an oath: they swore of their own accord, and so bound themselves twice over, since men who send for a prophet unasked can plead no excuse afterwards. He adds that nothing so confuses the mind and senses as hypocrisy, which alone makes men rush on to swear without dreading perjury.
7:
Why the answer waited ten days is the chief question, and five answer differently. Gill puts the delay to two ends, that it might carry greater weight and appear no device of the prophet's own, and chiefly to mortify an impatient people whose hypocrisy God knew and whose disobedience he foresaw; he denies the notion that the prophet spent the whole interval praying, holding rather that he laid the case before God and waited. Henry offers the same and adds another, that the delay showed the prophet did not speak of himself nor when he chose, and draws the lesson that we should keep waiting on God for direction, the vision being for an appointed time. Clarke turns it into doctrine, that prophets could no more prophesy at will than the disciples could work miracles at will, both gifts hanging on the will of the Most High and given only for the moment. Ellicott makes it deliberate reticence, the prophet refusing an answer of his own on the spur of the moment and waiting in prayer until there came into his mind what he could utter as an oracle, as an earlier prophet waited seven days; and notices the effect, that the suspense sharpened the eagerness of the crowd he addressed. Calvin distinguishes: on a common rule of life the prophet could have answered at once as an expounder of the law, but a special question required waiting, and the interval kept ostentation out and made the people receive the word as God's.

What the promise offers is read as accommodation. Calvin observes that a bare command would have sufficed, and that God let himself down to their infirmity by giving counsel and testifying it would be for their good, where orators can offer only conjectures; so their obstinacy added unbelief to contempt, and no greater reproach can be offered God than not to be believed. Ellicott hears in the building and planting the formulae with which the prophet's work began, and corrects the word for repenting, which means no regret for the past but a change of purpose from judgment to mercy; the counsel throughout is that they accept the punishment inflicted and stay as they are rather than seek safety in plans of their own devising. Wesley has God satisfied with what the nation has suffered and changing his providence for the rest. Henry adds the comparison that gives the promise its force, since their brethren had been carried off, so those who may stay should count it mercy and duty, never quitting that land while they can hold it.

Who is to show the mercy divides them. Calvin allows the words may mean God's own compassion and calls that the first ground of hope, but takes them rather of the king of Babylon, whose heart God would turn, since he shows mercies not only in forgiving but in inclining the hearts of men, and can make a father out of a savage wild beast; the passage teaches, he adds, that the purposes of men are governed from above. Keil and Delitzsch read it so too, that God would obtain compassion for them so the king would show pity. Ellicott is occupied instead with the promise of return, which may mean a carrying to Babylon followed by restoration, or immediate leave for the remnant to go back each to his own field; he prefers the second as suiting the prophet's aim, since a distant exile would hardly have persuaded them to stay.

Two observations close the tile. Calvin marks how carefully the delivery was made to leaders and people alike, so neither could plead the other's compulsion, and notes that the prophet presents the people's own prayer, acting as a middle person and asking nothing for himself. Henry makes the same point, the answer delivered publicly and faithfully, nothing kept back.
13:
Why the flight to Egypt is condemned is answered four ways. Calvin grounds it in the law, which had forbidden setting the heart on Egypt and had been confirmed often by the prophets, and adds that even a lawful thing would be diabolical presumption attempted against God's express will; he finds the root deeper, in a people who paid no regard to a favour freely promised, which is to charge God with falsehood while promising themselves rest where he had not offered it. Ellicott notes that the prophet had resisted an Egyptian alliance from first to last, and states the attraction with sympathy, since Egypt was still the granary of the East and its harvests made a bright contrast to the famine they had known. Clarke gives a reason none of the others does, that God knew their propensity to idolatry would make them take up the worship of the country. Keil and Delitzsch put the irony plainly, the very evil they feared at home overtaking them there.

The address to a remnant is calculated. Calvin makes the phrase a deliberate check, since men in prosperity are in a manner inebriated and hard to rule, the splendour of fortune making kings indulge themselves and private men lodge in their own dregs; the reminder of their humble condition was meant to make them teachable, though it bore no fruit.

Who falls under the sentence is worth Gill's qualification, that not everyone who went into Egypt is meant but everyone obstinately set on going, since some were carried there against their will, the prophet and his scribe among them. Ellicott suspects the words imply that others were taking the same course, something like a rush of fugitives from several nations looking to Egypt as their one hope; and notes that the warning gathers up the prophet's old phrases, so that by rejecting his counsel they involve themselves in the worst evils he ever prophesied. Clarke keeps it short and physical, the sword and the famine at their heels to overtake and destroy them. Calvin adds the force of the example before their eyes, since the man who threatens them had for years been the herald of a vengeance they had at last seen executed, which no other speaker could have said with the same authority.

Whom they deceived is uncertain in the Hebrew, and each takes it differently. Gill lays out the choices without settling them: they deceived the prophet, or their own souls, or used deceit to the hurt of their souls. Calvin rejects the first, since the prophet is not named in the clause, and prefers that they deceived themselves, the ungodly who affect astuteness weaving only snares for their own feet, so that craftiness always brings them to ruin. Ellicott asks how the prophet knew: looks and whispers may have betrayed his hearers, or he read their secret counsels by the intuition of inspiration, and what he read was a resolve to act as they liked, with his approval if it could be had and without it if not. Clarke does not analyse but exclaims, finding ingratitude, hypocrisy and rebellion enthroned in an incorrigible people.

The close seals the doom, and two dwell on the absurdity behind it. Clarke says that as they had determined to disobey, God has determined to punish, and confesses himself puzzled that men so disposed should trouble to inquire at all, unless out of curiosity, meaning to obey only if the answer fell in with their inclination. Calvin notices what they actually intended, not to settle in Egypt for good but to wait there until they might return, so wishing to be restored as it were against God's will while still putting his name forward. Gill closes on the justice of it, the prophet having sought the mind of the Lord at their own request and reported it faithfully.
